analysis.one_liner: Exempted drilling companies that passed safety checks from the post-spill offshore drilling moratorium.
analysis.headline: The bill sat on the Senate calendar for nearly six months without a vote and died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: In July 2010, two months after the BP Deepwater Horizon blowout spilled millions of gallons of oil into the Gulf of Mexico, the Interior Secretary had suspended most new offshore drilling and permitting. This bill would have let drilling companies escape that suspension if they had complied with two sets of new federal safety notices and passed all required inspections, and it would have forced the Interior Secretary to decide on their drilling permit within 30 days of finding them in compliance.
analysis.who_benefits: Offshore oil and gas drilling companies, and the Gulf businesses that supply them (rig crews, service vessels, equipment firms), because they could resume drilling and permitting months earlier than the moratorium allowed, with a guaranteed 30-day answer on each permit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Offshore drilling companies and their suppliers

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have applied the Interior Secretary's July 12, 2010 suspension of offshore permitting and drilling only to companies that had failed to comply with the June 8 and June 18, 2010 safety notices or had not completed required safety inspections [S3].

It would have required the Interior Secretary to make a decision on whether to issue a drilling permit within 30 days of finding an applicant in compliance with the safety notices and inspections, setting a firm clock on what was then an indefinite suspension [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If the bill had passed, the added risk would have fallen on Gulf coastal communities, fishing and seafood businesses, and coastal environments, because deepwater drilling would have restarted nationwide while the cause of the blowout and the adequacy of new safety rules were still being worked out, and the 30-day permit deadline would have limited how long regulators could study a specific application.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gulf coastal communities and fishing businesses

drawbacks.text: The bill would have restarted deepwater drilling across the Outer Continental Shelf for any company that filed the required paperwork and passed inspections, before the industry-wide review triggered by the Deepwater Horizon disaster was complete [S3].
The 30-day decision deadline would have pressured regulators to rule on permits quickly, limiting how much a specific well's risks could be examined before a decision [S2].

The strongest objection on the other side: the blanket moratorium itself had real costs, idling rigs and putting Gulf drilling-support workers out of work, and a compliant operator could argue it was being punished for an industry-wide failure. The bill addressed that by tying relief to the two new safety notices rather than repealing the moratorium outright [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded speed for caution. Getting Gulf drilling workers back on the job sooner was a real benefit, but the mechanism was to exempt individual companies from a safety suspension created after the worst offshore oil spill in U.S. history, and to put regulators on a 30-day clock. The safety case for keeping the moratorium until the new rules were tested was stronger, since no one knew yet whether the new notices would have prevented the blowout.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, read twice, and placed on the Senate's calendar of business in July 2010, but no vote was ever scheduled, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator David Vitter of Louisiana introduced the bill on July 14, 2010, for himself and with Senators John Cornyn and Roger Wicker [S3].

The bill would have limited the Interior Secretary's July 12, 2010 suspension of offshore permitting and drilling so it did not apply to applicants in compliance with new federal safety notices who had completed required safety inspections [S2].
The Senate read the bill a second time and placed it on the Legislative Calendar under General Orders on July 15, 2010 (Calendar No. 463) [S5].
The action history shows no further activity after that calendar placement — no committee hearing, no floor debate, no vote — through the end of the 111th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the drilling moratorium stood as issued and offshore drilling companies had to wait for it to be lifted through the administration's own process rather than by statute. Gulf coastal and fishing interests avoided a faster resumption of deepwater drilling; drilling companies did not get the earlier permits this bill would have guaranteed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The drilling moratorium stood; drillers had to wait

for.name: Sen. David Vitter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt compliant drillers from the offshore drilling moratorium and gave it a guaranteed 30-day permit clock.

for.name: Gulf Coast oil and gas drilling industry
for.what_they_did: Publicly pressed the administration and Congress to lift the deepwater drilling moratorium that had idled rigs and drilling-support jobs in the Gulf after the BP spill.

against.name: Senate Democratic leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the Senate floor and calendar
against.what_they_did: Left the bill on the Senate calendar after its second reading and never scheduled floor action, so it never received a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Gulf-state Republicans; with only 2 cosponsors out of 42 Senate Republicans and no Democrats signed on, and the Democratic-led Senate never acting on it, the fight followed party lines.

industries.note: The bill would have let drilling companies resume deepwater operations and get permit decisions within 30 days, months earlier than the post-Deepwater Horizon moratorium allowed. Their interest in restarting drilling faster ran against the public's interest in completing the industry-wide safety review after the largest offshore oil spill in U.S. history.

industries.industry: Offshore drilling support services (rig crews, service vessels, equipment suppliers)
industries.note: These businesses lost work while the moratorium idled rigs, and the bill would have put their employees back to work sooner. The benefit to Gulf workers was real, but it came by restarting the same activity under review after the blowout.
These industries bore the damage of the BP spill and depended on the water staying clean; a faster, looser path back to deepwater drilling would have exposed them to renewed spill risk.
